elements.text: In this lecture follow-up, we explore the generalized frog jump problem with variable jump size k, transitioning from recursive relations to optimized dynamic programming solutions.

elements.meaning: The minimum energy required for the frog to jump from the 0th index to the (n-1)th index.

elements.text: In Lecture 3, we were given a follow-up question where we had to find the minimum energy required for a frog to jump from the 0th index to the (n-1)th index, where the frog can jump from the ith index to i+1 and from i+1 to i+2.
The recurrence relation for this problem is f(i) = min(f(i-1) + |a[i] - a[i-1]|, f(i-2) + |a[i] - a[i-2]|).

elements.meaning: The recurrence relation for the frog to jump from the ith index to i+k, where k is a variable jump capacity.

elements.text: We can generalize the recurrence relation to allow the frog to jump from the ith index up to i+k, where k is any integer step up to the maximum jump limit.
We can convert the recurrence relation to a for loop, where we iterate from j = 1 to k and calculate the minimum energy required.

elements.meaning: The technique of storing the minimum energy required for each index to reduce the time complexity of the solution.

elements.text: We can use memoization to store the minimum energy required for each index, which will reduce the time complexity from exponential to polynomial.
The time complexity of the solution is O(n * k), where n is the number of indices and k is the maximum number of jumps.

elements.meaning: The technique of reducing the auxiliary space complexity from O(n) to O(k).

elements.text: We can optimize the space complexity of the solution from O(n) to O(k), but it is not necessary if k is equal or close to n.

In conclusion, we have solved the follow-up question of Lecture 3, derived the recurrence relation, generalized it for k jumps, converted it to an iterative DP solution, and analyzed time and space bounds.

points: Recurrence relation for frog jumping up to k steps
Converting recurrence to a bounded for-loop
Memoization table to prevent overlapping subproblems
Time complexity O(n*k) and space bounds
Space optimization possibilities down to O(k)
